title: Fen's Lost Map and the Grumpy Ogre
markdown:
In the gentle lands of Misty Kettle, where the air itself felt like a whispered secret, lived a young witch named Fen. Eyes like bright hazel nuts. Hair that looked spun from moonlight. How she loved secrets. Still learning charms, still remembering where to tuck her dragon scales. She had a rather wiggly talent for misplacing things, especially precious spell ingredients. Fairy dust here, dew from a moonlily there, and poof: gone like a wisp of smoke. Sometimes, when she tried to put her cat’s fur into a jar, it would simply vanish.

Her most faithful companion, and often her only witness, was Flicker: a baby griffin no bigger than a fluffy cushion, feathers the colour of a dove’s wing, eyes so large and round they seemed to hold all the world’s worries. Paws as soft as a kitten’s. Little wings fluttering with nervous energy at the slightest surprise. Quite the anxious little fluffball.

Today Fen’s hazel eyes were alight. “Flicker, my little cloud puff, today is the day. We are going to map the secret path that winds through the Whispering Pines. A path no one else knows. Our very own special adventure.”

Flicker let out a tiny anxious chirp. The Whispering Pines were deep, and deep meant new rustles, unknown shadows, rustlings that could sound like a ticklish caterpillar or a grumpy badger. He much preferred the cozy cottage, hearth a warm comforting glow, rustles only from spellbook pages. But Fen’s determination was like a warm sturdy hug. After a moment he chirped again, a little braver, tiny wings a hopeful twitch.

Satchel packed with charcoal sticks and tightly rolled parchment, they set off. Fen checked the satchel twice, then a third time, because ingredients had a habit of walking off when she was thinking of paths. Craggy familiar highlands melted into the hushed mysterious embrace of the deep woods. Sunlight dappled like scattered gold coins, dancing patterns on mossy ground. Damp earth and sharp pine needles, a perfume that made the nose tingle. Flicker stayed close enough that his wing brushed her sleeve at every unexpected rustle.

“This is it, Flicker.” Hushed with awe, eyes like tiny stars. “The adventure truly begins now.”

Just as she unfurled the parchment, a bold crimson leaf tinged with gold tumbled from a high branch, landed with a soft thump on Flicker’s delicate nose. Startled beyond measure, he sneezed. What a sneeze. The parchment, just loosened, fluttered from her grasp like a startled moth.

“Oh, Flicker.” Heart sinking. Caught by a mischievous gust, the parchment danced like a runaway kite, swirling toward a dense formidable thicket of thorny brambles that looked remarkably like a grumpy old man’s unkempt beard.

“My map.” Panic creeping. They peered at the prickly tangle. Retrieving it would be no easy feat. Fen tried a stick, then a longer stick, then the charcoal from her satchel, and each attempt only made the brambles close like a fist. Flicker chirped a warning every time a thorn snagged his feathers.

They tiptoed around the edges, Fen holding her breath, trying not to snag her cloak. The woods had gone quieter, as if even the gold-coin sunlight were waiting to see who would speak first. Then a low rumbling, distant thunder but much deeper, not thunder: a deep grumbly voice, thick with sleep and annoyance.

“Who’s disturbing my quiet? Who’s stirring up my peace?”

Emerging from behind a huge old oak: Maud, a gardener ogre, as big as a well-rounded boulder, nose like a large lumpy potato, green skin smudged with the rich dark soil of a beloved garden. Patched faded apron. Eyes large, always sleepy, undeniably grumpy.

“Excuse us. We’re just looking for our map. It blew away.”

Maud blinked watery eyes, taking in the young witch and fluffy companion. “Map? Paths? Bah. Disturbing my prize moonpetals? They’re not blooming properly, and it’s all this fuss. Making noise, breaking twigs.” A thick muddy finger toward sad droopy flowers, petals hanging limply.

Fen looked at the wilting moonpetals, pearly white dulled, then at Maud’s worried frown etched into a green brow. Not only their adventure. Someone else’s sadness. The grand plan suddenly a little inconsiderate. “I’m so sorry. We truly didn’t mean to bother you or your beautiful flowers.” A small stoppered vial in her satchel, a quick-fix for tired plants, brewed the other day. “Perhaps this might help?”

She uncorked and poured a few shimmering drops. Fizz. Pop. Instead of perking up, the flowers wilted more dramatically, pale petals a sickly jaundiced yellow. Flicker whimpered, wings tucked. Maud bellowed dismay. “You’ve made it worse. You’ve ruined them.”

True remorse. Not only a misplaced map: a distressed sleepy ogre and beloved flowers. Much harder than imagined. The vial went back into the satchel with a guilty click. Fen wiped her hands on her cloak as if the yellow wilt might come off her fingers.

Fen looked at the forlorn flowers, at Flicker’s wide worried eyes, at the cross ogre whose grumbles now sounded more like sighs. Sudden clarity, not of a secret path but of work that needed doing. “I don’t know precisely why your flowers are wilting, but I am a witch, and I want to help. We can find out what’s truly wrong.”

Maud looked genuinely surprised. Grumpiness softened a fraction. “Help? An ogre and a witch? Hmmph. That’s a new one.”

Fen knelt. Soil unusually dry, though it had rained recently. “The ground feels wrong.” Lessons about underground streams. “Perhaps the water isn’t reaching them properly.”

With Fen’s keen eye and Maud’s intimate knowledge of soil and hidden nooks, they dug carefully near the roots. The earth came up in dry crumbs at first, then cooler darker handfuls. Flicker, despite lingering nerves, nudged a small loose stone, revealing a faint almost imperceptible trickle. They followed it, widening the trench, Fen’s sleeves darkening, Maud muttering measurements under her breath as if the garden were a ledger. At last the culprit: a large heavy rock had fallen, blocking the underground stream that nourished the moonpetals.

“Aha.” Maud’s grumpiness forgotten, eager energy. “The stream. It was the stream all along.”

Together: Fen’s surprisingly strong small hands, Flicker nudging smaller pebbles with his beak, Maud’s immense strength. They braced, counted, and rolled the boulder aside until it settled with a damp thud among the oak roots. A gentle gurgle. Parched soil darkened with blessed moisture, the sound of water finding its old bed like a kettle coming to a quiet boil.

The sad droopy moonpetals began to unfurl, pale petals regaining pearly sheen, glowing softly, truly living up to their name. Fen sat back on her heels and let herself watch, because gardens, unlike maps, did not hurry.

Maud let out a long happy sigh. “They’re blooming. Thank you, young witch. You’ve saved them.” A wide crinkly smile that transformed the grumpy face.

Fen beamed. She hadn’t mapped a secret path as intended. She had helped a garden bloom. Flicker fluffed his feathers, pleased, nudged her hand.

“Now,” she said, twinkling, pulling out parchment she discovered had been tucked safely in her boot all along, “we can draw our path. But it will go gently around your beautiful garden. Quiet respect. Maybe even a little friendship.”

Maud chuckled, deep and rumbling, entirely friendly. “That’s a fine path. The best kind, I reckon.”

Sun descending, fiery orange and soft pink. Fen sat on a dry root and drew a new route winding past the radiant moonpetals along the peaceful edge of the woods, charcoal smudging her thumb. Flicker watched the lines as if they might vanish like fairy dust, then chirped, earlier worries forgotten. Maud brought a watering can she did not need, just to stand nearby while the stream did the work. The map, when Fen looked, had a garden on it instead of a secret. The moonpetals’ scent followed them home, which was how you knew a sneeze could lose a parchment and a boulder could still be rolled aside.
characters: Fen (young witch who misplaces spell ingredients), Flicker (an anxious baby griffin)
